lan: Local Area Network: a network that covers a small area such as a home, school or office.
A small network that connects the devices that are close to each other.
The Wi-Fi network in your house that links your phone, laptop and printer.
wan: Wide Area Network: a network that connects LANs across a large geographic area, such as cities or countries.
A very big network that joins many smaller networks far apart.
A bank linking its branches in different cities.
router: A device that forwards data between networks and connects a local network to the internet.
The traffic director of your home network: it decides where data should go.
The box that gives your phone and laptop their Wi-Fi and internet access.
modem: A device that converts the signal from your internet provider into data your network can use, and back again.
The doorway between your home and your internet company.
The box connected to the fiber, cable or phone line coming into the house.
switch: A device that connects several wired devices on a LAN and sends data only to the device it is meant for.
A smart power strip for network cables that sends each message to the right computer.
The box in a school lab that connects 24 desktop computers.
ethernet: A standard for wired network connections using cables, usually fast and stable.
A network cable that plugs into a computer.
A cable between a desktop computer and the router.
wi-fi: A wireless technology that connects devices to a network using radio waves.
A way to connect to the network without a cable.
Connecting your phone to the home network in the living room.
ip address: A number that identifies a device on a network so data can be delivered to it.
The home address of a device on a network.
192.168.1.10 is a typical address of a device on a home network.
dns: Domain Name System: a service that translates website names into IP addresses.
The phone book of the internet: you give it a name and it gives back the number.
Turning example.com into the address your browser can connect to.
packet: A small piece of data sent across a network, with information about where it comes from and where it goes.
A tiny envelope of data. Big messages are split into many envelopes.
A photo sent to a friend is cut into many packets and put back together on arrival.
server: A computer that provides pages, files or services to other devices.
A computer that answers when other computers ask for something.
The computer that sends you a web page when your browser asks for it.
isp: Internet Service Provider: a company that gives you access to the internet.
The company you pay to get internet at home.
A telephone or fiber company that sells home internet.
wpa2: A common Wi-Fi security standard that encrypts traffic between your device and the router. WPA3 is newer and stronger.
A secret lock on your Wi-Fi so that strangers cannot read your messages.
Choosing WPA2 or WPA3 in your router settings instead of leaving Wi-Fi open.
access point: A device that lets Wi-Fi capable devices join a wired network (LAN) wirelessly.
The spot that sends out the Wi-Fi signal so your phone can join the network.
A ceiling-mounted Wi-Fi unit in a school corridor.
gateway: A device that connects a local network to other networks, such as the internet, and forwards traffic between them.
The door that your home network uses to reach the outside world.
A provider box that works as modem and router together.
https: HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure: web communication that is encrypted while it travels.
A locked way of talking to a website so people along the way cannot read your messages.
The padlock in the address bar when you log in to a website. It protects the connection but does not prove the site is honest.
